children: By Erin Mulvaney and Cara Lombardo
Michael Aiello was near the pinnacle of the legal world.

A go-to adviser for marquee corporate mergers, he had risen to become Weil Gotshal & Manges' largest revenue generator and highest-paid partner, making north of $20 million a year, according to people familiar with the matter. He wielded significant sway over the direction of the firm for nearly two decades and oversaw a more than 600-person team.
But some partners felt for years he hoarded resources and stifled plans to grow in other areas, some of the people said. Several partners began to consider leaving for rival firms.

It turns out Aiello was looking at the exit door, too. The star lawyer and five of his allies are decamping to Cravath, Swaine & Moore, The Wall Street Journal reported this week, part of a raft of seismic defections in the world of Big Law as firms try to find their footing in an industry under pressure.

The legal industry as a whole hasn't grown dramatically over the past decade, meaning the work has become more concentrated among a smaller group of elite firms that have largely opted for scale. Retaining talent and clients is getting harder and the potential of artificial intelligence to replace work done by lawyers is a gathering threat.

While both Weil and Cravath have been losing ground to larger rivals such as Kirkland & Ellis, they are taking decidedly different strategies. Cravath, which itself has struggled to retain talent, has intentionally eschewed scale even as many peers go global.

Weil, meanwhile, has an ambitious plan to further expand across practice areas, including into its lucrative private-equity and restructuring practices, a strategy that Aiello supported but feared would potentially erode the culture of the close-knit firm, people familiar with the matter say. The latest departures, on top of others the Journal reported recently, have many of Weil's rivals on Wall Street debating its future.

The upheaval comes at a sensitive time, as the firm is in the middle of a major leadership transition. Boston partner Ramona Nee is set to take over in January for longtime leader Barry Wolf, an ally of Aiello and one of his closest friends. While Aiello helped tap Nee, who is embracing growth, he eventually started eyeing an exit for a boutique more in line with his ethos, according to people familiar with the matter. Senior partners knew about his frustration for years.
"The question is, can they make up for the loss of Mike? Or could this be taking the shackles off and growing in a different direction?" said Robert Kinney, a recruiter who has been working for Weil.

Aiello informed Weil's leadership he was leaving this week. The firm issued a terse statement Thursday, saying he and others were leaving for a "smaller platform," and referencing the firm's ambitious growth strategy.
Weil made its name shepherding companies including Lehman Brothers and Enron through bankruptcies and has recently poached partners focused on private equity and restructuring.

But rebuilding after the recent departures is likely to require landing high-profile hires or, potentially, merging with a competitor. The firm is actively recruiting lateral partner groups and would be open to any options for growth, but isn't in active discussions for a merger, people familiar with the matter say.
Divergent visions
Known both for his charm and intensity, Aiello, 57 years old, has been a polarizing force at Weil since he rejoined in 2007 from Dewey Ballantine.

He has been in the thick of some of the biggest M&A standoffs in history, including helping Disney fend off a hostile takeover from Comcast and Dow Chemical's $130 billion merger with DuPont-and its subsequent dismantling.

At times, Aiello clashed with other partners who weren't a fan of his management style. More recently, colleagues complained that Aiello, based in New York, seemed distracted by traveling to tend to Cesena FC, the Italian soccer team he and an investor group took a stake in several years ago.
Kinney, the recruiter, said Aiello's presence made it hard to hire new partners for Weil's Texas office, a major initiative for the firm, after prospects cited concerns about working in his shadow.

By mid-August, two groups of top private-equity focused lawyers were in talks to leave, one for Paul Weiss and another for Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. Christopher Machera, the former co-head of Weil's private-equity group and a former member of its management committee, has since joined Paul Weiss.
Defections, particularly of high-profile partners, can create anxiety among lawyers who fear such changes could affect their firms' financial standing.

Top lawyers have been switching allegiances at an unprecedented pace. A group of six litigators left Wachtell earlier in the summer in an almost unheard-of move. The British firm Linklaters nabbed three partners from Paul Weiss as part of a bid to expand in the U.S.

Aiello started to increasingly feel like he was living in limbo at Weil and word began spreading that he could be open to finding a landing spot at another firm, according to people familiar with the matter. Some of the smaller firms briefly considered making a run at him, the people said, but not every firm was willing to hire several other partners, too.

Roughly a month ago, he met Faiza Saeed, Cravath's longtime leader and a decadeslong friend, for a regularly scheduled lunch. They connected over Saeed's vision for Cravath to remain a boutique firm focused on high-profile M&A, such as Paramount's planned $81 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, and litigation. Saeed has said many of her larger competitors do commoditized work in comparison.
Yet, hiring a splashy lateral group was a stark departure from Cravath's homegrown ethos.

Founded in 1819, Cravath built a prestigious reputation and preferred to build talent from "cradle to grave" with its own training method. Unlike its peers racing to open hubs around the world, it maintains small presences in select locations.

Also unlike almost every other firm on Wall Street, Cravath for years resisted changing its lockstep compensation system, which pays partners on a rigid payscale based largely on seniority. That has put the firm at a disadvantage to rivals that could pay top lawyers millions more, setting off a wave of departures that began with its star dealmaker Scott Barshay in 2016.

In 2021, Cravath announced plans to modify its compensation system, which kept lockstep largely in place, but allowed 15% of its profits to be divided among its highest performers. The firm started more frequently managing partners out or reducing their equity in some instances. Their lockstep system gives the most senior partners about three times what new partners make, not including any bonuses for high performers.
People familiar with the matter said Cravath plans to pay Aiello close to what he was making at Weil, but not more.
